A study is undertaken to evaluate a new serological screening test for the diagnosis of tuberculosis infection. In the study, 1000 people were randomly selected from the population and given the new diagnostic test, and positive and negative results were recorded. Each study participant also was given the gold standard diagnostic procedure to determine the true infection state of the individual. The findings are as follows:

Which of the following is the positive predictive value of the screening test under study?

explanations.A: Sensitivity and specificity are useful for assessing the validity of a test. 130/180 is the sensitivity of the test.
explanations.D: 760/810 is the negative predictive value of the test.

generalExplanation:
Although predictive values are not true indices of the validity of a test, these are still of prime importance to physicians. In clinical practice, patients will more often present with a positive or negative test result, rather than a disease or disease-free state; therefore, one should have sufficient knowledge about the predictive values of a test.

Positive predictive value is defined as the proportion of subjects with a positive test result who actually have the disease. Negative predictive value is defined as the proportion of subjects with a negative test result who are free of disease. Consider the following 2 x 2 table:

Positive predictive value = TP/(TP+FP) or A/(A+B)
Negative predictive value = TN/(TN+FN) or D/(C+D)
In this case, the PPV is 130 / 190.
educationalObjective: Know how to calculate the predictive values of a test.

stem:
A group of scientists developed a new test to diagnose fibromyalgia. They conducted a study to evaluate the performance of the test in a sample of 2,500 subjects where 5% had a confirmed diagnosis of fibromyalgia. The initial results of the study are shown below.

Which of the following would result in an increase of the ratio of true positives to all positive tests?

explanations.A: Predictive values do not depend on the size of the study sample; instead, they depend on the prevalence of disease in the sample.
explanations.B: A less-sensitive test will reduce the number of TPs but will have no effect on the number of FPs; therefore, PPV will decrease.
explanations.C: Similarly, a less-specific test will have no effect on the number of TPs but will increase the number of FPs; therefore, PPV will decrease.

generalExplanation:
FN = false negative; FP = false positive; NPV = negative predictive value; PPV = positive predictive value; TN = true negative; TP = true positive.

The positive predictive value (PPV) is the probability that an individual truly has a disease given a positive test result. PPV is equal to the number of individuals with the disease who test positive (ie, true positive [TP]) divided by all those with a positive test result (ie, TP + false positive [FP]). It is calculated as:
PPV = TP / (TP + FP)

Similarly, negative predictive value (NPV) is equal to the number of individuals without the disease who test negative (ie, true negative [TN]) divided by all those with a negative test result (ie, TN + false negative [FN]), calculated as: NPV = TN / (TN + FN).

Predictive values depend on disease prevalence in a population of interest. Specifically, disease prevalence affects PPV by changing TP and FP.
• Populations with low disease prevalence have more TN and fewer TP. In such populations, more positive tests would have more FP with fewer FN. This explains why NPV increases (ie, more TN, fewer FN) and PPV decreases (ie, fewer TP, more FP) with decreasing prevalence.
• Populations with high disease prevalence have more TP and fewer TN. In such populations, more negative tests would have more FN with fewer FP. This explains why NPV decreases (ie, fewer TN, more FN) and PPV increases (ie, more TP, fewer FP) with increasing prevalence.

In this case, a new test to diagnose fibromyalgia is evaluated in a study sample of 2,500 subjects where 5% had a confirmed diagnosis of fibromyalgia. This means that the test was evaluated in a study sample with a low prevalence of disease. Therefore, one way to increase the PPV of the test would be to evaluate the test in a sample from a population with a higher prevalence of disease (eg, high-risk population).
educationalObjective: Predictive values change depending on the disease prevalence in a study population. As disease prevalence increases, the positive predictive value increases and the negative predictive value decreases.

stem: A study is conducted to determine whether there is an association between congenital heart disease (CHD) and pediatric stroke. A total of 420 children with a history of ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke and 1,260 age-matched children with no history of stroke participate in the study. The study results show that CHD is an important childhood risk factor for stroke, and that children who undergo surgical repair for CHD remain at elevated risk outside the perioperative period. The study concludes that children with CHD would benefit from optimized long-term stroke prevention strategies. Which of the following statements is most likely true about this study design?

options.A: Congenital heart disease is the only risk factor for stroke that the study is able to evaluate
options.B: Ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke is the only outcome that the study is able to evaluate
options.C: The results of the study could be greatly biased due to disproportionate loss to follow-up
options.D: The study is likely time-consuming and costly because it requires measuring time to stroke

explanations.A: Once participants are categorized based on disease status, investigators can evaluate past exposure to ≥1 risk factors of interest (eg, congenital heart disease [CHD]) in each group.
explanations.C: In case-control studies, exposure status to risk factors is typically assessed immediately after subjects have been categorized based on outcome/disease status, so this study design does not require a follow-up (ie, no disproportionate loss to follow-up between cases and controls).
explanations.D: Therefore, case-control studies are usually less time-consuming and less costly compared to other study designs (eg, cohort studies, randomized trials).

generalExplanation:
This study has a case-control design in which participants are initially selected based on their status for a particular disease: case (ie, history of ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke) or control (ie, no history of ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke).
• Because cases and controls are categorized based on their status for a particular disease, a case-control study is able to evaluate only a single outcome (ie, stroke).
• Once participants are categorized based on disease status, investigators can evaluate past exposure to ≥1 risk factors of interest (eg, congenital heart disease [CHD]) in each group (Choice A).

These features make case-control studies useful to study diseases that are rare or that have a long latency period between exposure and clinical presentation.
educationalObjective: Case-control studies can consider only 1 outcome (ie, disease) per study but can evaluate exposure to ≥1 risk factors.

stem: A group of medical geneticists conducts a study to detect microRNA-29a (miR-29a) expression in the plasma of patients with lumbar spinal stenosis (LSS) and to investigate the clinical significance. Specimens are collected from patients with LSS, patients with lumbar intervertebral disc herniation, and healthy people. Reverse transcription-quantitative polymerase chain reaction analysis is used to detect expression levels of miR-29a in plasma. Several studies on neuromuscular disease models have shown an association between levels of miR-29a and those of matrix metalloproteinase 9 (MMP-9) and a disintegrin and metalloproteinase with thrombospondin motifs 5 (ADAMTS-5), so western blot is used to detect the expression levels of MMP-9 and ADAMTS-5 protein. Study results reveal that the correlation between the expression levels of miR-29a and MMP-9 is −0.94 (p < 0.01), and that the correlation between the expression levels of miR-29a and ADAMTS-5 is −0.55 (p < 0.01). Based on these results, which of the following statements is most correct?

options.A: A low expression of miR-29a in plasma is a statistically significant cause for low expression of MMP-9 and ADAMTS-5 in plasma
options.B: About 94% of the variation in the expression levels of MMP-9 and 55% of the expression levels of ADAMTS-5 are explained by the expression levels of miR-29a in plasma
options.C: Lower expression levels of miR-29a in plasma tend to relate to higher levels of expression of MMP-9 and ADAMTS-5 in plasma, and vice versa
options.D: There is a statistically significant positive linear relationship between expression levels of miR-29a and expression levels of MMP-9 and ADAMTS-5 in plasma
options.E: There is not a statistically significant linear relationship between expression levels of miR-29a and expression levels of MMP-9 and ADAMTS-5 in plasma

explanations.A: However, a significant linear relationship between 2 variables does not necessarily imply causality.
explanations.B: The values −0.94 and −0.55 are correlation coefficients; they describe the direction and strength of the linear relationship between 2 quantitative variables. The statistic that describes the percentage of variation in a variable that is explained by another variable is the coefficient of determination, which in many cases is equal to the square of the correlation coefficient (r², also known as r-squared).
explanations.D: Both correlation coefficients are negative (ie, r < 0) and statistically significant (ie, p < 0.05); therefore, there is a significant negative linear relationship between expression levels of miR-29a and expression levels of MMP-9 and ADAMTS-5 in plasma.
explanations.E: Both correlation coefficients are negative (ie, r < 0) and statistically significant (ie, p < 0.05); therefore, there is a significant negative linear relationship between expression levels of miR-29a and expression levels of MMP-9 and ADAMTS-5 in plasma.

generalExplanation:
The correlation coefficient (r) describes the direction (ie, negative, positive) and the strength (ie, values closer to 1 indicate stronger relationships) of the linear relationship between 2 quantitative variables, as follows:
• r < 0 indicates that, as one variable increases, the other variable decreases. This means that lower values of one variable tend to relate to higher values of the other variable, and vice versa.
• r > 0 indicates that both variables increase (or decrease) together. This means that lower values of one variable tend to relate to lower values of the other variable, and vice versa.

In this study, results reveal that the correlation between expression levels of microRNA-29a (miR-29a) and matrix metalloproteinase 9 (MMP-9) in plasma is −0.94 (p < 0.01), and that the correlation between miR-29a and a disintegrin and metalloproteinase with thrombospondin motifs 5 (ADAMTS-5) in plasma is −0.55 (p < 0.01). Both correlation coefficients are negative (ie, r < 0) and statistically significant (ie, p < 0.05); therefore, there is a significant negative linear relationship between expression levels of miR-29a and expression levels of MMP-9 and ADAMTS-5 in plasma (Choices D and E).

This means that as expression levels of miR-29a increase, expression levels of MMP-9 and ADAMTS-5 decrease. As a result, lower expression levels of miR-29a in plasma tend to relate to higher levels of expression of MMP-9 and ADAMTS-5 in plasma, and vice versa. However, a significant linear relationship between 2 variables does not necessarily imply causality (Choice A).
educationalObjective: The correlation coefficient (r) describes the direction (ie, positive, negative) and strength of the linear relationship between 2 quantitative variables. It does not necessarily imply causality.

stem:
Researchers at a large pharmaceutical company discover a tumor-specific antigen present in high quantities in the serum of patients with pancreatic cancer. A study is then performed to evaluate serum levels of the tumor marker in patients with and without the disease. The following curves are generated using the results of the study.

The drug company decides to utilize the newly discovered tumor antigen by creating a screening test for pancreatic cancer. During preliminary design of the test, the cutoff point for positive/negative results is set at point B. If the cutoff point is moved from B to A, the sensitivity of the screening test will change in which of the following ways?

explanations.A: Moving the cutoff point from B to A will cause more patients with the disease to test positive (fewer FNs), increasing the sensitivity of the test.
explanations.B: Moving the cutoff point from B to A will cause more patients with the disease to test positive (fewer FNs), increasing the sensitivity of the test. Conversely, moving the cutoff point in the other direction (eg, A to B) would decrease sensitivity while increasing specificity.
explanations.D: Moving the cutoff point from B to A will cause more patients with the disease to test positive (fewer FNs), increasing the sensitivity of the test.

generalExplanation:
• False positive (FP) - A patient with a positive test result who actually does not have the disease.
• True negative (TN) - A patient with a negative test result who actually does not have the disease.
• False negative (FN) - A patient with a negative test result who actually has the disease.
• Sensitivity - The number of patients correctly testing positive for a disease divided by the total number of patients with the disease (TP / [TP + FN]). High sensitivity means that negative results are less likely to be FNs and more likely to be TNs; thus, a negative result is better able to rule out the disease (SnOut). Because tests with high sensitivity will correctly identify most of the patients with the disease, sensitivity is very important for screening tests (which need to minimize FNs).
• Specificity - The number of patients correctly testing negative for a disease divided by the total number of patients without the disease (TN / [TN + FP]). High specificity means that positive results are less likely to be FPs and more likely to be TPs; thus, a positive result is better able to rule in the disease (SpIn). Because tests with high specificity will correctly identify most of the patients without the disease, specificity is very important for confirmatory tests (which need to minimize FPs).

In this example, moving the cutoff point from B to A will cause more patients with the disease to test positive (fewer FNs), increasing the sensitivity of the test. However, as a consequence, more patients without the disease will also test positive (more FPs), resulting in decreased specificity. Conversely, moving the cutoff point in the other direction (eg, A to B) will increase the number of FNs and decrease the number of FPs, decreasing sensitivity while increasing specificity.
educationalObjective: Changing the cutoff point of a quantitative diagnostic test will inversely affect its sensitivity and specificity. Typically, lowering the cutoff value will increase sensitivity (fewer false negatives) and decrease specificity (more false positives). Screening tests need high sensitivity, and confirmatory tests need high specificity.

stem: A large study is conducted to assess the association between altitude and life expectancy. Researchers obtained data on life expectancy at the county level from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and collected altitude data from the US Geological Survey. A regression was used to model the association between altitude and life expectancy at the county level in 3,064 counties in the contiguous US while also controlling for several well-established covariates. Which of the following best describes the design of this study?

explanations.A: Cohort and cross-sectional studies deal with individuals rather than populations. In cohort studies, individuals with and without different exposures (eg, residing in high- or low-altitude locations) are followed over time to compare outcomes (eg, life expectancy).
explanations.B: In cross-sectional studies, individuals are assessed for exposure to risk factors and disease simultaneously at a given point in time ("snapshot") to determine whether risk factors are associated with disease (at the individual level). The overall design of this multicounty study relies on population-level data, not individual-level data.
explanations.D: Qualitative studies use focus groups, interviews (structured and semi-structured), and other anthropologic techniques to obtain narrative information for explaining quantitative results.
explanations.E: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses combine the results of several published studies (with an emphasis on high-quality, randomized controlled studies) to estimate the pooled effect.

generalExplanation:
In this study, researchers collected:
• county-level data on life expectancy from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and
• altitude data from the US Geological Survey
to determine whether altitude is associated with life expectancy.

Using population-level (eg, county, state, country), rather than individual-level, data as a unit of analysis in such a manner is consistent with an ecological study. Ecological studies are useful for generating hypotheses but should not be used to draw conclusions regarding individuals within these populations because statistical relationships observed in a population (ie, a collection of individuals) may not hold true within all of the subgroups that make up that population.

For example, this study may show that altitude is significantly associated with longer life expectancy at the county level when, in fact, altitude is significantly associated with shorter life expectancy in certain groups within a county (eg, people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease). This apparent paradox is known as ecological fallacy.
educationalObjective: In ecological studies, the unit of observation is the population, not the individual. Disease rates and exposures are measured in each of a series of populations and their associations determined. Results about associations at the population level may not translate to the individual level.

stem: The neurorehabilitation unit at a local hospital conducted a randomized controlled trial to compare the effects of high-intensity treadmill training (HITT) against low-intensity treadmill training (LITT) on gait ability, quality of life, cardiorespiratory fitness, and cost of walking in patients with chronic stroke. Thirty patients were randomized to either HITT or LITT, but 9 patients in the HITT group and 3 patients in the LITT group dropped out of the study. The statistical analysis was conducted following a per-protocol principle. Based on this information, which of the following is of most concern regarding the analysis?

options.A: It will increase the chance of differential dropouts between intervention groups
options.B: It will misrepresent the effect of the intervention among patients of a medical practice
options.C: It will not estimate the effect of the intervention in patients who completed the study
options.D: It will only estimate the effect of assigning the intervention to patients
options.E: It will result in a more conservative estimate of the effect of the intervention

explanations.A: Participants drop out of a study before any statistical analysis is conducted, so the type of statistical analysis does not affect the dropout rates in a study.
explanations.C: Per-protocol (PP) analysis provides an estimate of the effect of an intervention assuming an (unrealistic) perfect scenario in which all participants were retained and completed treatments as planned.
explanations.D: An intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis estimates the effect of assigning (rather than receiving) an intervention.
explanations.E: Compared to PP analysis, ITT analysis could lead to a more conservative estimate of the effect of the intervention.

generalExplanation:
Study dropouts may bias estimates of treatment effect. For example, in a placebo-controlled, randomized trial of interventions (ie, high-intensity treadmill training [HITT] group vs low-intensity treadmill training [LITT] group), adverse effects on health may cause a greater proportion of patients with more severe illness to drop out from the HITT group than from the LITT group. This means that at the trial's conclusion, the HITT group may have a smaller proportion of more severely ill patients than the LITT group (eg, selection bias). This could distort the estimation of the effect of the interventions (eg, confounding bias).

Per-protocol (PP) analysis compares treatment groups in a randomized trial by including in the analysis only those participants who strictly adhered to and completed the protocol (ie, it excludes dropouts). Therefore, it provides an estimate of the effect of an intervention assuming an (unrealistic) perfect scenario in which all participants were retained and completed treatments as planned (Choice C). However, clinical settings (eg, medical practices) almost inevitably include dropouts, so PP analysis misrepresents (typically overestimates) the effect of the intervention.

In contrast, an intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis includes all participants as initially allocated after randomization, regardless of what happens during the study period (eg, keeping the HITT and LITT dropouts in their respective groups for analysis). ITT analysis estimates the effect of assigning (rather than receiving) an intervention; compared to PP analysis, ITT analysis could lead to a more conservative estimate of the effect of the intervention (Choices D and E). However, it closely mirrors the expected number of dropouts in a real-life situation, so ITT analysis reflects the (realistic) expected effect of the intervention in a medical practice setting.
educationalObjective: Per-protocol analysis includes only those participants who strictly adhered to and completed the study protocol (ie, nondropouts). This approach tends to provide an estimate of the true effect of an intervention for a perfect scenario, but it can overestimate the effect of the intervention in a practical clinical setting.

stem: A group of physicians wants to determine the relationship between metabolic anomalies and moyamoya disease (MMD), a chronic cerebrovascular occlusion disorder that may lead to ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke. Based on data suggesting that serum uric acid and triglycerides may both be associated with vasoocclusion, the physicians design a study to investigate whether, in individuals newly diagnosed with MMD, serum uric acid levels are independently related to serum triglyceride levels after adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics, BMI, smoking status, and alcohol consumption. Three hundred individuals are recruited, and quantitative levels of serum uric acid and triglycerides are measured at baseline. Which of the following is the best statistical technique to answer the research question?

explanations.A: The analysis of variance (ANOVA) compares the mean of a quantitative dependent variable in several independent groups. For example, ANOVA could be used to compare mean serum triglyceride level in patients with low, normal, or high serum uric acid levels (3 groups).
explanations.C: Odds ratio (OR) and relative risk (RR) measure the strength of association between 2 categorical variables: a categorical risk factor (eg, smoker or nonsmoker) and a categorical outcome or disease (eg, presence or absence of myocardial infarction). The OR is used in case-control studies, and the RR is used in cohort studies.
explanations.D: Odds ratio (OR) and relative risk (RR) measure the strength of association between 2 categorical variables: a categorical risk factor (eg, smoker or nonsmoker) and a categorical outcome or disease (eg, presence or absence of myocardial infarction). The OR is used in case-control studies, and the RR is used in cohort studies.

generalExplanation:
Variables are broadly classified as qualitative (ie, categorical) or quantitative (eg, continuous) based on their scale of measurement. Qualitative variables (eg, type of treatment, blood type) represent categories or groups, whereas quantitative variables (eg, temperature, glucose level) represent numerical values. The scale of measurement of the dependent (eg, outcome) and independent (eg, exposures, risk factors) variables in a study determines the correct statistical test.

Regression analysis is used to describe the association between 1 quantitative dependent variable (eg, outcome) and ≥1 independent variables (eg, exposures, risk factors), which may be quantitative or qualitative, while adjusting for other variables of interest. In this study:
• The 1 quantitative dependent variable is serum triglyceride level.
• The independent variable is serum uric acid level (1 quantitative independent variable).
• The association between the main independent variable (eg, serum uric acid) and the dependent variable (eg, serum triglyceride) is adjusted to account for the effects of other independent variables referred to as adjustment variables or covariates (eg, sociodemographic characteristics, BMI, smoking status, alcohol consumption). Controlling for these variables reduces potential confounding.

Calculation of a regression line (eg, line of best fit) can then determine whether serum uric acid level has a statistically significant association with serum triglyceride level (after adjusting for covariates). In this study, uric acid level is considered the independent variable (ie, independently related to triglyceride level); however, an equivalent relationship could have been studied using triglyceride level as the independent variable. In both instances, the best statistical technique is linear regression.
educationalObjective: A regression analysis is a statistical technique used to describe the effect of ≥1 independent variables (eg, exposures, risk factors), which may be quantitative or qualitative, on 1 quantitative dependent variable (ie, outcome).

stem: A case-control study was conducted to assess the relationship between alcohol consumption and breast cancer. First, the investigators interviewed patients with breast cancer. They then selected the neighbors of the patients with the same age and race, and used them as controls. Such study design helps to control which of the following problems?

explanations.A: Selection bias is not controlled by matching, because the controls selected may not reflect the exposure experience (in this case, alcohol consumption) of the general population.
explanations.B: Recall bias, observer's bias, and ascertainment bias result from mislabeling exposed/unexposed or cases/controls. These are not affected by matching.
explanations.C: Recall bias, observer's bias, and ascertainment bias result from mislabeling exposed/unexposed or cases/controls. These are not affected by matching.
explanations.D: Recall bias, observer's bias, and ascertainment bias result from mislabeling exposed/unexposed or cases/controls. These are not affected by matching.

generalExplanation:
Matching is an efficient method to control confounding. It is frequently used in case-control studies. The initial step involves the selection of matching variables, which should always be the potential confounders (e.g., age, race). Cases and controls are then selected based on the matching variables, such that both groups have a similar distribution in accordance with the variables.

In this scenario, neighborhood "controls" were matched to "cases" by age and race. Selecting neighbors as controls has another advantage of matching the cases to controls by variables that are difficult to measure (e.g., socioeconomic status).
educationalObjective: Matching is frequently used in case-control studies because it is an efficient method to control confounding. Remember: matching variables should always be the potential confounders of the study (e.g., age, race). Cases and controls are then selected based on the matching variables, such that both groups have a similar distribution in accordance with the variables.

stem: A 72-year-old woman diagnosed with osteoporosis and recovering from a recent vertebral fracture caused by a fall is concerned about future vertebral fractures. She reads a magazine article on how drug Z reduces the risk of new fractures in patients with osteoporosis by 60%. The report states that patients in the study were randomly assigned to either the new drug or placebo. The incidence of new fractures in the drug Z group was 10% whereas in the placebo group it was 25%. Which of the following was most likely presented as the 60% reduction in fractures?

explanations.B: The number needed to treat (NNT) is the number of patients who need to be treated with a specific treatment (eg, drug Z) to prevent an additional negative event (eg, 1 fewer patients with a new vertebral fracture) when compared with a control group (eg, placebo). NNT is the inverse of the absolute risk reduction (ARR): NNT = 1 / ARR. In this study, NNT = 1 / 0.15 = 6.7 (or 7).
explanations.C: The odds ratio measures the strength of the association between a risk factor (eg, smoker or nonsmoker) and an outcome/disease (eg, presence or absence of myocardial infarction) in case-control studies.
explanations.D: RR = (Risk_treatment / Risk_control) = (0.10 / 0.25) = 0.40.

generalExplanation:
Absolute risk reduction (ARR) describes the absolute difference in risk of an unfavorable outcome between the treatment group (eg, drug Z) and the control group (eg, placebo):
ARR = (Risk_control − Risk_treatment)

Relative risk reduction (RRR) describes the difference in risk of an unfavorable outcome between the treatment group and the control group relative to the control group and calculated as follows:
RRR = ARR / Risk_control

In this example, Risk_control (ie, risk of new vertebral fracture in the placebo group) is 0.25 (or 25%), and Risk_treatment (ie, risk of new vertebral fracture in the drug Z group) is 0.10 (or 10%). Therefore, ARR and RRR for new vertebral fractures among patients in the drug Z group are:
ARR = 0.25 − 0.10 = 0.15 (or 15%) (Choice A)
RRR = 0.15 / 0.25 = 0.60 (or 60%)

Alternately, RRR may be calculated using relative risk (RR):
RRR = 1 − RR
For this example, RR is the ratio of the risk of new vertebral fractures in drug Z group to the risk of new vertebral fractures in the placebo group:
RR = (Risk_treatment / Risk_control) = (0.10 / 0.25) = 0.40 (Choice D)
Therefore, RRR = 1 − 0.40 = 0.60 (or 60%).

Advertisements sometimes report RRR rather than ARR to give the appearance of a more substantial effect, as in this case with 60% (relative) reduction as compared to 15% (absolute) reduction.

Note: The formula for RRR based on RR can be derived from the formula for RRR based on the difference in risks, as follows: RRR = (Risk_control − Risk_treatment) / Risk_control = 1 − (Risk_treatment / Risk_control) = 1 − RR. Risk_control and Risk_treatment are sometimes called the control and treatment rates, respectively.
educationalObjective:
Relative risk reduction (RRR) measures how much a treatment reduces the risk of an unfavorable outcome. RRR may be calculated using the absolute risk reduction (ARR) or the relative risk (RR):
• RRR = ARR / Risk_control = (Risk_control − Risk_treatment) / Risk_control
• RRR = 1 − RR

stem: A clinical trial is conducted to assess the effectiveness of a new drug for migraine headache. As part of the trial design, researchers set the statistical probability values for alpha and beta at 0.05 and 0.10, respectively, and a sample of 800 adult patients with chronic migraines, selected from patients who attend headache clinics at several major academic medical centers, are randomly assigned to receive the new drug or placebo. Baseline scores on a standardized migraine disability assessment tool are obtained. Analysis of the results after 6 months of treatment shows that the new drug is associated with a clinically significant improvement in scores on the assessment tool, with a p-value of 0.04. Which of the following parameters would most likely have been greater if the study had been conducted using 300 subjects?

options.A: Likelihood of a type I error
options.B: Likelihood of a type II error

explanations.A: Therefore, a reduction in sample size results in a greater probability of a type II error and a lower probability of a type I error (known as alpha [α]).
explanations.C: Sensitivity and specificity are performance parameters of a diagnostic test. Sensitivity is defined as the percentage of diseased individuals who are correctly identified (ie, proportion of subjects who have a positive test result among all those with disease). Specificity is defined as the percentage of healthy individuals who are correctly identified (ie, proportion of subjects who have a negative test result among all those without disease). This study is not evaluating the performance of a diagnostic test.
explanations.D: Sensitivity and specificity are performance parameters of a diagnostic test. Sensitivity is defined as the percentage of diseased individuals who are correctly identified (ie, proportion of subjects who have a positive test result among all those with disease). Specificity is defined as the percentage of healthy individuals who are correctly identified (ie, proportion of subjects who have a negative test result among all those without disease). This study is not evaluating the performance of a diagnostic test.
explanations.E: A study with a smaller sample size (eg, 300) would have had a lower power to detect such a difference if one truly existed.

generalExplanation:
A type II error occurs when a false null hypothesis H0 is not rejected, that is, when a study does not find a statistically significant difference although one truly exists (ie, false negative). The probability of a type II error (known as beta [β]) is the complement of statistical power (1 − β). Statistical power is the probability of rejecting a false H0, that is, the ability to find a statistically significant difference when one truly exists (ie, true positive).

The power of a study is affected by its sample size. Studies with larger sample sizes have greater power to detect differences between groups when one truly exists than do studies with smaller sample sizes. This means that studies with smaller sample sizes have a greater probability of a type II error than do studies with larger sample sizes. Type I errors (ie, a true H0 is rejected, resulting in a false positive) and type II errors are typically inversely related to each other—as one increases, the other decreases. Therefore, a reduction in sample size results in a greater probability of a type II error and a lower probability of a type I error (known as alpha [α]).

In this example, results show that the new drug for migraines is clinically and statistically better than placebo in a study of 800 patients. A study with a smaller sample size (eg, 300) would have had a lower power to detect such a difference if one truly existed (Choice E). Subsequently, the study with the smaller sample size also would have had a greater probability of a type II error; it would also have resulted in a lower probability of a type I error (Choice A).
educationalObjective: Studies with larger sample sizes have greater power (ie, a false H0 is rejected) and therefore lower probability of a type II error than do studies with smaller sample sizes.

stem: A prospective cohort study was conducted to evaluate the long-term effects of a high-fat diet on the incidence of colon cancer. The study participants were randomly selected from the population of interest. Dietary patterns were assessed through the use of periodic self-completed questionnaires. The investigators reported a 5-year relative risk of 1.60 for people who consumed a high-fat diet compared to individuals who consumed a low-fat diet. The 95% confidence interval was 1.02 to 2.15. This study is most likely to have which of the following p values?

explanations.B: These p values are all > 0.05, meaning the associated 95% confidence interval would contain the null value.
explanations.C: These p values are all > 0.05, meaning the associated 95% confidence interval would contain the null value.
explanations.D: These p values are all > 0.05, meaning the associated 95% confidence interval would contain the null value.
explanations.E: These p values are all > 0.05, meaning the associated 95% confidence interval would contain the null value.

generalExplanation:
Relative risk (RR) is the probability of the outcome of interest occurring in the exposed group compared to the probability of it occurring in the non-exposed group. The null value of the RR is 1.0; a RR of 1.0 means that the outcome occurs with equal frequency in both groups and that there is no association between the exposure and the outcome. A RR > 1.0 means that the outcome occurs more frequently in the exposed group (positive association). The RR says nothing about the statistical significance of a study.

Statistical significance can be expressed with either p values or confidence intervals, but both are interrelated. For instance, p < 0.05 corresponds to a 95% confidence interval that does not contain the null value. Likewise p < 0.01 is equivalent to a 99% confidence interval that does not contain the null value. Conversely, if the null value is within a given confidence interval, then the p value is ≥ the equivalent confidence interval.

In general, for study results to be statistically significant, the 95% confidence interval must not contain the null value. This is equivalent to p < 0.05, which means that there is less than a 5% chance that the results are due to chance alone. In this case, the 95% confidence interval is 1.02 to 2.15 and does not contain the null value of 1.0. This corresponds to p < 0.05, thus 0.04 is the only correct answer choice.
educationalObjective: Confidence intervals and p values are interrelated and express the statistical significance of a study. In a statistically significant study, p should be < 0.05. This corresponds to a 95% confidence interval that does not include the null value.

stem: A prospective cohort study was conducted to assess the effects of oral contraceptive (OC) use on the incidence of breast cancer. A crude analysis of the study suggests an association between OC use and breast cancer (relative risk [RR] = 1.40, 95% confidence interval [95%CI]: 1.01, 1.96). Further analysis shows that in women with a family history of breast cancer, OC use increases the risk of breast cancer (RR = 3.33, 95%CI: 2.51, 4.41). In women without a family history of breast cancer, a significantly smaller effect is observed (RR = 1.27, 95%CI: 1.01, 1.60). The results of this study are best explained by which of the following?

explanations.A: Given that the measures of association are significantly different from one another at the strata level (RR = 3.33 [95%CI: 2.51, 4.41] vs RR = 1.27 [95%CI: 1.01, 1.60]), BC family history is not a confounder.
explanations.C: Latency period is the time required for a given exposure to have a measurable effect on the outcome. This study provided no information on how long oral OCs must be used to have an effect on BC risk in susceptible patients.
explanations.D: Observer bias and selection bias are errors in study design involving misclassification of data and inappropriate selection of participants, respectively.
explanations.E: Observer bias and selection bias are errors in study design involving misclassification of data and inappropriate selection of participants, respectively.

generalExplanation:
Effect modification (interaction) results when an extraneous variable (modifier) changes the direction or strength of an association between a risk factor and a disease. A modifier is associated with the disease but not the risk factor. Effect modification can sometimes be confused with confounding, the bias that results when the exposure-disease relationship is obscured by the effect of an extraneous factor (confounder) associated with both exposure and disease.

Stratified analysis by the extraneous variable can help distinguish whether that variable is a confounder or an effect modifier, as follows:
• Confounder (left panel): The measures of association (eg, relative risk [RR] of bladder cancer among alcohol users) calculated in each of the stratified groups (eg, smokers and nonsmokers) are similar to one another (eg, nonstatistically significant RR = 0.95 [95%CI: 0.51, 1.76] and RR = 1.03 [95%CI: 0.34, 3.13]), but they differ from the measure of association calculated in the crude analysis (eg, statistically significant RR = 1.81 [95%CI: 1.06, 3.10]); stratification can remove the effects of the confounder (eg, smoking).
• Effect modifier (right panel): The measures of association calculated in each of the strata are significantly different (in strength or direction) from one another; stratification can make the effects of the modifier more apparent.

In this example, family history of breast cancer (BC) modifies the association between oral contraceptive (OC) use and BC. Crude analysis reveals a significant association (ie, RR = 1.40 [95%CI: 1.01, 1.96]) between OC use and BC. However, once the association is stratified by family history of BC, the strength of the association changes (ie, with BC family history, RR = 3.33 [95%CI: 2.51, 4.41]; with no BC family history, RR = 1.27 [95%CI: 1.01, 1.60]), reflecting a significantly higher risk for BC among those who take OCs if they also have a positive BC family history. In other words, positive BC family history acts as an effect modifier.
educationalObjective: Effect modification results when an external variable positively or negatively impacts the effect of a risk factor on the disease of interest. Stratified analysis helps determine whether a variable is a confounder or an effect modifier.

stem:
A prospective cohort study is conducted to compare the rates of medication errors, adverse drug events (ADEs), and potential ADEs in pediatric and adult hospital settings. The first cohort consists of 1,120 pediatric patients admitted to a pediatric institution, and the second cohort consists of 1,281 adult patients admitted to an adult institution. Both cohorts were followed-up for 12 weeks. A total of 10,778 medication orders from the pediatric institutions and 10,070 medication orders from the adult institutions were reviewed in the study. Rate of medication errors and ADEs are summarized in the graph below.

Which of the following approximates the relative probability of potential ADEs in the pediatric institution compared to the adult institution?

explanations.B: 0.75 is the rate difference of potential ADEs between the adult institution and the pediatric institution expressed as a percentage: RD_adult, pediatric = Rate_adult − Rate_pediatric = 1.1% − 0.35% = 0.75%. However, the question asks for RR_pediatric vs adult.
explanations.C: 0.93 is the RR of medication errors (rather than potential ADEs) in the pediatric institution compared to the adult institution (5.30% / 5.70% = 0.93).
explanations.D: 1.04 is the RR of ADEs (rather than potential ADEs) in the pediatric institution compared to the adult institution (0.25% / 0.24% = 1.04).
explanations.E: 3.14 is the RR of potential ADEs in the adult institution compared to the pediatric institution: RR_adult vs pediatric = 0.011/0.0035 ≈ 3.14 (or 314%). However, the question asks for RR_pediatric vs adult, which is the inverse of RR_adult vs pediatric.

generalExplanation:
This is an example of a cohort study in which 2 different cohorts (eg, patients admitted to a pediatric institution, patients admitted to an adult institution) are followed across time (eg, 12 weeks) to estimate and compare the rate of an outcome of interest (eg, potential adverse drug events [ADEs]).

A common measure used to estimate the relative probability (ie, chance) of an outcome of interest in cohort studies is the relative risk (RR). RR is equal to the rate of an outcome (eg, potential ADEs) in one cohort (eg, pediatric institution) divided by the rate of the same outcome in a second cohort (eg, adult institution):
RR_pediatric vs adult = Rate_pediatric / Rate_adult

In this case, RR_pediatric vs adult must be calculated based on the data shown on the given graph. The graph reported the following rates of potential ADEs in both institutions:
• Rate of potential ADEs in the pediatric institution: Rate_pediatric = 0.0035 (or 0.35%)
• Rate of potential ADEs in the adult institution: Rate_adult = 0.011 (or 1.10%)

Therefore, RR_pediatric vs adult = (0.0035 / 0.011) ≈ 0.32. This indicates that the rate of potential ADEs in the pediatric institution is a third that in the adult institution; more precisely, the rate of potential ADEs is 68% (ie, 100% − 32%) lower in the pediatric institution compared to the adult institution.
educationalObjective: When comparing the relative risk (RR) of the same outcome in 2 cohorts: RR = rate of outcome in cohort 1 / rate of outcome of cohort 2.

stem: A neurologist researching patients with stroke wants to study the association between cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) concentrations of T-tau as an explanatory variable and brain atrophy (measured quantitatively using 2 outcome variables: ventricular volume and total brain volume) 1 year poststroke. A total of 210 patients with first-ever ischemic stroke or transitory ischemic attack without preexisting cognitive impairment are included in the study. After 12 months, CSF biomarkers (including T-tau protein levels) are assessed. In addition, subjects undergo MRI, and brain atrophy is estimated based on calculations of ventricular CSF volume and total brain volume normalized for subject head size. Which of the following is the best statistical technique to describe the association between the explanatory and the outcome variables?

explanations.A: The analysis of variance (ANOVA) compares the mean of a quantitative dependent variable in several independent groups. For example, ANOVA could be used to compare mean serum triglyceride level in patients with low, normal, or high serum uric acid levels (3 groups).
explanations.B: The chi-square test evaluates the association between 2 categorical variables, as in a study evaluating the association between sex (male, female) and myocardial infarction (presence, absence).
explanations.D: Odds ratio (OR) and relative risk (RR) measure the strength of the association between 2 categorical variables: a categorical explanatory variable (eg, smoker, nonsmoker) and a categorical outcome or disease (eg, presence or absence of myocardial infarction). The OR is used in case-control studies, and the RR is used in cohort studies.
explanations.E: Odds ratio (OR) and relative risk (RR) measure the strength of the association between 2 categorical variables: a categorical explanatory variable (eg, smoker, nonsmoker) and a categorical outcome or disease (eg, presence or absence of myocardial infarction). The OR is used in case-control studies, and the RR is used in cohort studies.

generalExplanation:
Variables are broadly classified as qualitative (ie, categorical) or quantitative (eg, continuous) based on their scale of measurement. Qualitative variables (eg, type of treatment, blood type) represent categories or groups whereas quantitative variables (eg, temperature, glucose level) represent numeric values. The scale of measurement of the dependent (eg, outcome) and independent (eg, explanatory) variables in a study determines the correct statistical test.

Linear regression analysis is used to describe the association between:
• 1 quantitative dependent (ie, outcome) variable. In this study, brain atrophy (evaluated using 2 quantitative variables: ventricular volume and total brain volume) is the quantitative outcome variable.
• ≥1 independent (ie, explanatory) variables, which may be quantitative or qualitative. In this study, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) concentration of T-tau is a quantitative explanatory variable.

A regression analysis can determine whether CSF concentration of T-tau (explanatory variable) is significantly associated with brain atrophy (outcome variable). However, given that the study measures brain atrophy through 2 different variables (ie, ventricular volume, total brain volume), 2 different regression models are required: one to evaluate the association between CSF concentrations of T-tau and ventricular volume and one to evaluate the association between CSF concentrations of T-tau and total brain volume. Regression analyses may or may not adjust for other variables of interest.
educationalObjective: A regression analysis is a statistical technique used to describe the effect of ≥1 independent variables (eg, exposures, risk factors), which may be quantitative or qualitative, on 1 quantitative dependent variable (ie, outcome).

stem: A single-blind randomized controlled trial is conducted to determine whether a novel treatment for moderate to severe (ie, not controlled adequately by topical therapies) eczema is more effective than dupilumab in reducing the clinical symptoms. Eighty adults with moderate to severe eczema are randomly assigned to receive the new treatment or dupilumab every 2 weeks for 16 weeks. Treatment effectiveness is based on physician and patient reports of symptom improvement. Results based on physicians' reports suggest that the novel treatment is more effective than dupilumab in improving symptoms (p = 0.02). Results based on patients' reports suggest that the novel treatment is as effective as dupilumab in improving symptoms (p = 0.15). Which of the following is of greatest potential concern in this study?

options.A: Many severe cases were lost to follow-up only in the novel treatment group
options.B: Patients had an inaccurate recollection of the effectiveness of the treatment
options.C: The effect of the treatment is different for different age groups
options.D: The outcome in this specific study design is subjective in nature
options.E: The study only included patients with moderate to severe eczema

explanations.A: An unequal loss of participants from study groups in follow-up (eg, cohort, experimental) studies is known as attrition bias. The study in this question provides no information to evaluate attrition.
explanations.B: Inaccurate recollection of past events, known as recall bias, is a potential problem for case-control studies (not randomized controlled trials), particularly when questionnaires are used to ask participants about distant past exposure.
explanations.C: Effect modification occurs when an external variable differentially modifies (positively or negatively) the effect of a treatment on the outcome of interest in different groups. In this study, participants were randomly assigned to treatments, so effect modification by age is very unlikely.
explanations.E: The study evaluates a novel treatment for moderate to severe eczema. Therefore, a sample composed of patients with moderate to severe eczema is adequate and not a concern in this study.

generalExplanation:
Observers (eg, researchers, physicians) in a study may introduce bias by misclassifying data (eg, treatment outcomes) due to individual differences in interpretation or preconceived expectations regarding the treatment. This type of bias is known as observer bias. It is a concern in single-blind studies, in which individuals observing outcomes are aware of treatment assignments, and in studies that rely on subjective outcomes (eg, symptoms improvement).

This question describes a single-blind study in which physicians responsible for reporting subjective outcomes (ie, eczema symptoms improvement) were unblinded to (aware of) treatment assignments whereas participants were blinded to (unaware of) treatment assignment. Study results based on physicians' reports show that the novel treatment is more effective; however, study results based on patients' reports show that the treatments are equally effective. These results suggest that a preconceived expectation regarding the novel treatment and knowledge of treatment assignment may have led some physicians to overestimate symptoms improvement and effectiveness of the novel treatment compared to dupilumab. This is an example of observer bias.
educationalObjective: Observer bias occurs when observers (eg, researchers, physicians) misclassify data (eg, treatment outcomes) due to preconceived expectations regarding the treatment. This type of bias may lead to an underestimation or overestimation of a treatment effect.

stem: A group of researchers at a university hospital plans to conduct a study to investigate the association between diagnosis of schizophrenia or bipolar disorders and acute myocardial infarction (AMI). They plan to use hospital administrative data to identify adult patients who were diagnosed with schizophrenia or bipolar disorder between 2008 and 2010. A second group of age- and sex-matched patients without a diagnosis of schizophrenia or bipolar disorder during the same period will also be selected. The researchers then plan to examine medical records to determine whether patients with a diagnosis of schizophrenia or bipolar disorders were more likely to have had an AMI over the 10-year period after the schizophrenia or bipolar disorder diagnosis. Based on this information, which of the following best describes this study design?

explanations.A: Case-control studies begin by identifying participants based on outcome status (eg, cases who have had AMI vs controls who have not had AMI), whereas this study initially identified participants based on exposure status.
explanations.B: Case series and cross-sectional studies are examples of descriptive observational designs. This study examines the association between a risk factor (eg, diagnosis of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder) and outcome (eg, AMI), making it an analytical design.
explanations.C: Case series and cross-sectional studies are examples of descriptive observational designs. This study examines the association between a risk factor (eg, diagnosis of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder) and outcome (eg, AMI), making it an analytical design.
explanations.D: In a prospective cohort design, the study begins before the outcome has occurred (ie, occurrence of disease in exposed and nonexposed groups is assessed prospectively).

generalExplanation:
Observational studies are broadly classified as having a descriptive or analytic design.
• Descriptive designs (eg, case report, case series, cross-sectional) describe patterns of disease in populations by time, place, and person. These studies help generate hypotheses about associations between risk factors and disease, such as in a study showing that a high proportion of people with lung cancer are also smokers.
• Analytical designs (eg, case-control, cohort, some cross-sectional designs) test hypotheses about associations between risk factors and disease, such as in a study that determines that smoking is a statistically significant risk factor for lung cancer.

This study is an example of a cohort study, an observational analytical design in which potential participants are initially identified as "exposed" or "nonexposed" according to exposure status to a risk factor (eg, diagnosis of schizophrenia or bipolar disorder between 2008 and 2010). Once participants are categorized based on exposure status, the occurrence (ie, incidence) of the outcome (eg, acute myocardial infarction [AMI]) within a specific time period (eg, 10 years) is determined and compared between groups to estimate the association between risk factor and outcome. Cohort studies may be either prospective or retrospective:
• In a retrospective cohort design, the study begins after the outcome has occurred (ie, occurrence of disease in exposed and nonexposed groups is assessed retrospectively), as in this study, which collects data on the occurrence of AMI from a review of medical records (ie, after AMI had occurred).
• In a prospective cohort design, the study begins before the outcome has occurred (ie, occurrence of disease in exposed and nonexposed groups is assessed prospectively) (Choice D).
educationalObjective: A cohort study begins by identifying individuals as exposed or nonexposed to a risk factor and ends by comparing outcome (ie, disease) rates between the exposed and nonexposed groups. In a prospective cohort design, the study begins before the outcome has occurred, whereas in a retrospective cohort design the study begins after the outcome has occurred.

stem: A 55-year-old man recently diagnosed with adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC) visits his oncologist to discuss treatment options. The patient lives a very healthy lifestyle and wonders what might have triggered the development of this rare type of cancer that has a prolonged latent period. He asks the physician about risk factors for ACC. Which of the following is the most appropriate study design to answer the patient's question?

explanations.B: Descriptive designs (eg, case report, case series, cross-sectional study) describe patterns of disease in populations by time, place, and person. In this question, the patient was diagnosed with a rare type of cancer (adenoid cystic carcinoma, ACC) and asks about risk factors for ACC. This means that the study must be analytical (ie, able to test hypotheses about associations between risk factors and ACC).
explanations.C: Descriptive designs (eg, case report, case series, cross-sectional study) describe patterns of disease in populations by time, place, and person. In this question, the patient was diagnosed with a rare type of cancer (adenoid cystic carcinoma, ACC) and asks about risk factors for ACC. This means that the study must be analytical (ie, able to test hypotheses about associations between risk factors and ACC).
explanations.D: A cohort study initially identifies individuals based on exposure status to a risk factor and then follows both groups over time to assess the development of disease. This study design is inefficient to study uncommon diseases or diseases with a long latent period because a considerable amount of time is necessary for some disease to occur, and the likelihood that a sufficiently large number of individuals will develop the disease to draw any valid conclusions is very low.
explanations.E: A cross-sectional study takes a snapshot of a population to estimate the prevalence of risk factors and disease simultaneously, so it is unlikely that this study design will capture sufficient cases of a rare disease to draw any valid conclusions.

generalExplanation:
Observational studies are broadly classified as having a descriptive or analytical design:

These studies help generate hypotheses about associations between risk factors and diseases, such as a study showing that a high proportion of people with lung cancer are also smokers.

In this question, the patient was diagnosed with a rare type of cancer (adenoid cystic carcinoma, ACC) and asks about risk factors for ACC. This means that the study must be analytical (ie, able to test hypotheses about associations between risk factors and ACC) (Choices B and C).

A case-control study is an analytical design in which potential participants are initially identified based on disease status as cases (ie, with disease) or controls (ie, without disease). Once cases and controls are identified, the presence of past exposure to ≥1 risk factors of interest is determined in each group. Because individuals have been deliberately chosen based on disease status, this study design is particularly efficient and cost-effective to study uncommon (rare) diseases with a long latent period (ie, time between exposure and disease occurrence), such as ACC.
educationalObjective: The case-control study is the most appropriate analytical design to study uncommon (rare) diseases and diseases with a long latent period.

Title
Postoperative acute renal failure (ARF) in pediatric patients undergoing cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB).

Objective
To identify risk factors associated with postoperative ARF according to the Pediatric Risk, Injury, Failure, Loss, End-Stage Renal Disease (pRIFLE) scale in children undergoing cardiac surgery with CPB.

Methods
Design: Case-control study.
Participants: 455 children age <16 who were admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit after cardiac surgery that required CPB. Cases were patients who developed some degree of ARF according to pRIFLE criteria (n = 155); controls were patients who did not develop ARF (n = 300).
Exposure: Cardiac surgery requiring CPB.
Outcome: Pediatric postoperative ARF.

Results
Bivariate and multivariate analyses (adjusted for age, sex, and CPB duration) are shown below.
*Unadjusted analysis.
**Adjusted for age, sex & duration of CPB.
CI = confidence interval; CPB = cardiopulmonary bypass; OR = odds ratio.

Conclusion
The study identified several independent risk factors associated with the development of postsurgical ARF.

---

The abstract shown on the left applies to the next 2 items.

A 4-year-old girl is monitored at the hospital after undergoing cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) to repair an acyanotic congenital heart defect. The procedure required aortic clamping, and CPB lasted 150 minutes. Maximal lactatemia during CPB was 7 mmol/L, and laboratory studies showed moderate metabolic acidosis. The patient subsequently develops postoperative ARF.

Item 1 of 2
Based on the abstract, which of the following was the most significant risk factor that contributed to this patient's developing postoperative ARF?

explanations.A: Cyanotic heart disease: OR = 3.62; 95% CI: 1.11-11.63 (cyanotic heart defect is a risk factor, ie, acyanotic heart defect is a protective factor).
explanations.B: The CIs for CPB duration, metabolic acidosis, and aortic clamping in the multivariable (adjusted) analysis include the null value (OR = 1.0), so those risk factors are not statistically associated with ARF.
explanations.D: The CIs for CPB duration, metabolic acidosis, and aortic clamping in the multivariable (adjusted) analysis include the null value (OR = 1.0), so those risk factors are not statistically associated with ARF.
explanations.E: The CIs for CPB duration, metabolic acidosis, and aortic clamping in the multivariable (adjusted) analysis include the null value (OR = 1.0), so those risk factors are not statistically associated with ARF.

generalExplanation:
The odds ratio (OR) is a measure of association used in case-control studies to compare the odds of exposure in cases (ie, individuals with disease) relative to controls (ie, individuals without disease):
OR = (odds of exposure in cases) / (odds of exposure in controls)

ORs may be unadjusted or adjusted:
• An unadjusted OR estimates the association between a risk factor and an outcome but does not account (ie, control) for the effect of other variables, known as potential confounders (eg, patient demographics, clinical factors), on the outcome of interest.
• An adjusted OR accounts for the effect of potential confounders, thereby minimizing confounding and providing better estimates of associations.

A confidence interval (CI) that includes the null value (ie, OR = 1.0) is not statistically significant, and a CI that excludes the null value is statistically significant.

This study provides unadjusted (bivariate) and adjusted (multivariable) ORs for several risk factors among patients who developed ARF (cases) compared to patients who did not (controls). Unadjusted analysis shows that all risk factors are significantly associated with ARF (ie, CIs exclude the null value). However, once potential confounders (ie, age, sex, duration of CPB) are controlled in the adjusted analysis, the only statistically associated risk factors (ie, CIs exclude the null value) are:
• Moderate-to-severe hyperlactatemia: OR = 4.91; 95% CI: 1.26-19.05
• Cyanotic heart disease: OR = 3.62; 95% CI: 1.11-11.63 (Choice A)

The CIs for CPB duration, metabolic acidosis, and aortic clamping in the multivariable (adjusted) analysis include the null value (OR = 1.0), so those risk factors are not statistically associated with ARF (Choices B, D, and E). This implies that the variables controlled for in the adjusted analysis were distorting the true association between the risk factors and the outcome.

Based on these results, this patient's maximal lactate level of ≥6 mmol/L (ie, moderate-to-severe hyperlactatemia) is a risk factor for developing postoperative ARF; cyanotic heart defect is also a risk factor (ie, acyanotic heart defect is a protective factor).
educationalObjective: The odds ratio (OR) is a measure of association between an exposure and an outcome. Confidence intervals that contain the null value (ie, OR = 1.0) indicate that the association is not statistically significant. Adjusted ORs minimize confounding and provide better estimates of associations.

---

Item 2 of 2
Based on the abstract, which of the following is of most concern regarding this study?

options.A: Differential mortality between cases and controls
options.B: Lack of power to detect any statistical associations

explanations.A: Differential mortality refers to differences in death rates between specific groups participating in follow-up studies (eg, randomized controlled trials, cohort studies). Because this is a case-control study, patients are not followed across time and differential mortality is not applicable.
explanations.B: Failure to show a statistically significant association between a risk factor and an outcome is often due to insufficient power (eg, due to a small sample size) to detect an association. However, this study showed several statistically significant associations after adjusting for age, sex, and duration of CPB, suggesting sufficient power to detect these significant associations. Additional statistically significant associations may be identified with a larger sample size (ie, more power) but would not negate established associations.
explanations.D: Misclassification of cases occurs when the outcome (eg, disease) is not assessed correctly. In this case-control study, cases were patients who developed ARF according to pRIFLE criteria, which standardize ARF classification based on creatinine clearance. Therefore, cases are clearly defined and less likely to be misclassified.

generalExplanation:
Confounding bias occurs when a study does not control for extraneous variables independently related to both the risk factor and the outcome. When not controlled, confounders may mask the true effect that the independent variable has on the dependent variable, which may lead to false conclusions (ie, statistically significant results that are truly invalid).

In this study, a bivariate (ie, unadjusted) analysis was conducted to identify potential risk factors for ARF among children undergoing surgery with CPB. A multivariable (adjusted) analysis was also conducted to control for the effects of age, sex, and duration of CPB on the relationship between the risk factors (ie, aortic clamping, cardiac output syndrome, hyperlactatemia during CPB, metabolic acidosis, type of heart disease) and the outcome (ie, ARF). However, there may be other important risk factors for ARF after CPB that the multivariable analysis did not control for, such as preoperative creatinine level, proteinuria, albuminuria, or ACE inhibitor use. Therefore, limited adjustment for potential confounders may have led to residual confounding in the study.
educationalObjective: Confounding bias occurs when an extraneous (ie, confounding) variable masks the relationship between an independent variable (eg, risk factor, treatment) and a dependent variable (ie, outcome, disease of interest). It may lead to false conclusions (ie, statistically significant results that are truly invalid). Failure to adjust for potential confounding factors may lead to residual confounding and a distortion of the true relationship between variables.

stem: A large, multicenter study was conducted to determine the efficacy of pegfilgrastim, a new drug developed to reduce the risk of febrile neutropenia (FN) in patients with early-stage breast cancer. One thousand women age 40-69 with stage I-III invasive breast carcinoma who were scheduled to receive cyclophosphamide-based chemotherapy were enrolled in the study and randomly assigned to receive either placebo (500 women) or pegfilgrastim (500 women) at a dose previously shown in a small trial to have biological activity. Results showed that the incidence of FN was significantly lower in the pegfilgrastim group than in the placebo group, and that patients in the pegfilgrastim group required fewer hospitalizations and lower antibiotic usage related to FN. Most adverse events were consistent with those expected for breast cancer subjects receiving cyclophosphamide-based chemotherapy. Researchers concluded that pegfilgrastim is safe and significantly reduces the incidence of FN in breast cancer patients. Which of the following best describes this type of study?

explanations.A: New treatments go through several research phases: some phases involve no human subjects (ie, preclinical studies).
explanations.B: A phase I trial assesses toxicity, maximum tolerated dose, adverse effects, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics of a new treatment, usually in a small number of healthy subjects. This study involved a large sample of affected patients and was aimed at assessing efficacy.
explanations.C: A phase II trial assesses efficacy, optimal dosing, and adverse effects of a new treatment in a small (rather than a large) number of affected patients (ie, patients with the disease of interest). Some phase II trials may have ≥1 group, but these are generally small in sample size.
explanations.E: A phase IV trial studies adverse effects caused over time by a new treatment after it has been approved and is on the market, as in a study to assess long-term adverse effects related to use of pegfilgrastim in breast cancer patients.

generalExplanation:
The clinical trials process addresses whether new treatments (eg, drugs, procedures) are effective and safe for their intended use (eg, treatment of disease) in the target population (eg, patients with the disease of interest). New treatments go through several research phases: some phases involve no human subjects (ie, preclinical studies) (Choice A); and some involve few (ie, phase I and II trials) or many (ie, phase III and IV trials) human subjects.

A phase III trial assesses treatment efficacy and human safety (eg, evaluates long-term or rare adverse effects). It compares a new treatment to standard treatments (or placebo) in a large sample of affected patients (ie, patients with the disease of interest). Most phase III trials are randomized and blind (ie, patients/researchers are unaware of treatment assignment), and may compare ≥2 treatments. Results determine whether a new treatment is approved by the Food and Drug Administration for a commercial market.

In this question, the study evaluated the efficacy of a new treatment (ie, pegfilgrastim) in reducing the risk of disease (ie, febrile neutropenia) in affected patients (ie, early-stage breast cancer) who were randomly assigned to the new treatment compared to placebo. This process is consistent with a phase III trial.
educationalObjective: Phase III trials evaluate the efficacy, risks, and benefits of a new treatment compared to current standard treatments (or placebo) in a large sample of affected patients (ie, patients with the disease of interest). Most phase III trials are randomized, blind, and compare ≥2 treatments.

Title
Alcohol, smoking, and caffeine in relation to fecundability and NAT2

Objective
To investigate how alcohol, smoking, and caffeine associate with fecundability and determine whether the most common polymorphisms in the N-acetyltransferase 2 (NAT2) metabolic enzyme help explain these associations.

Methods
Design: Prospective study of fertility and menstrual function. Follow-up for an average of eight menstrual cycles.
Participants: 295 women age 20-41 at risk for pregnancy.
Exposure: Caffeine categorized into mean caffeine intake <300 mg/day and ≥300 mg/day. Alcohol categorized into <1 drink/day and ≥1 drinks/day. Smoking categorized into smokers and nonsmokers. NAT2 acetylator status categorized into slow and rapid NAT2 acetylator phenotypes.
Outcome: Fecundability.

Results
In general, fecundability was not associated with caffeine (odds ratio [OR] = 0.89; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.58 to 1.38) or current smoking (OR = 1.04; 95% CI: 0.65 to 1.67). Alcohol use was significantly associated with reduced fecundability (OR = 0.50; 95% CI: 0.28 to 0.89). However, the associations were inconsistent across NAT2 status. NAT2 status alone was not significantly associated with fecundability (OR = 1.44; 95% CI: 0.89 to 2.35).

Conclusion
This research suggests the need to incorporate genetic information about metabolic enzymes to better interpret and understand the effects of xenobiotics on human health.

---

The abstract shown on the left applies to the next 2 items.

A 28-year-old primigravida woman comes to the office due to inability to conceive despite appropriately timed, unprotected intercourse for the past 6 months. The patient has had no abnormal Pap tests. She and her husband have no chronic medical conditions or previous surgeries. The patient does not use alcohol or illicit drugs. She drinks >1 cup of coffee per day and is a moderate smoker. Blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg, and pulse is 68/min. BMI is 23 kg/m². Physical examination reveals a soft, nontender abdomen with no masses. The patient's N-acetyltransferase 2 (NAT2) acetylator status is unknown.

Item 1 of 2
Which of the following conclusions can be drawn from the results of the study?

options.A: Alcohol has a significant effect on fecundability among rapid acetylators
options.B: Fecundability is significantly associated with NAT2 status
options.C: The effect of smoking and alcohol on fecundability is modified by NAT2 status
options.D: There is a significant association between caffeine and fecundability regardless of NAT2 status

explanations.A: Among rapid acetylators, fecundability was not significantly associated with caffeine, alcohol, or smoking because all CIs included the null value of OR = 1 (95% CI: 0.50 to 1.85 for NAT2/caffeine; 95% CI: 0.61 to 2.22 for NAT2/alcohol; 95% CI: 0.93 to 2.94 for NAT2/smoking).
explanations.B: Based on the abstract, fecundability is not significantly associated with caffeine or NAT2 status because the corresponding CIs included the null value (95% CI: 0.58 to 1.38 for the association between fecundability and caffeine; 95% CI: 0.89 to 2.35 for the association between fecundability and NAT2 status).
explanations.D: Based on the abstract, fecundability is not significantly associated with caffeine or NAT2 status because the corresponding CIs included the null value (95% CI: 0.58 to 1.38 for the association between fecundability and caffeine; 95% CI: 0.89 to 2.35 for the association between fecundability and NAT2 status).

generalExplanation:
This study evaluated how caffeine, alcohol, and smoking associate with fecundability in women age 20-41 at risk for pregnancy. The initial results (ie, unstratified analysis) show that fecundability is significantly associated with alcohol (ie, confidence interval [CI] for the odds ratio [OR] excluded the null value [OR = 1]) but not with caffeine or current smoking (ie, CIs included the null value). A subsequent stratified analysis was conducted based on participants' N-acetyltransferase 2 (NAT2) acetylator phenotypes to determine whether NAT2 status (ie, slow or rapid acetylation) helps explain these associations. The stratified analysis shows that some of these associations were inconsistent across NAT2 status (ie, slow or rapid acetylators).

• Among slow acetylators, fecundability was significantly associated with alcohol and smoking because the CIs excluded the null value of OR = 1 (95% CI: 0.07 to 0.56 for NAT2/alcohol; 95% CI: 0.23 to 0.48 for NAT2/smoking). However, fecundability was not significantly associated with caffeine because the CI included the null value of OR = 1 (95% CI: 0.67 to 1.62 for NAT2/caffeine).
• Among rapid acetylators, fecundability was not significantly associated with caffeine, alcohol, or smoking because all CIs included the null value of OR = 1 (95% CI: 0.50 to 1.85 for NAT2/caffeine; 95% CI: 0.61 to 2.22 for NAT2/alcohol; 95% CI: 0.93 to 2.94 for NAT2/smoking) (Choice A).

Therefore, the effect of smoking and alcohol on fecundability is modified by NAT2 status—NAT2 status is an effect modifier. Effect modification (interaction) occurs when an extraneous variable (effect modifier) changes the effect an exposure (eg, treatment) has on an outcome in certain groups of individuals but not others. A stratified analysis based on the modifier can help detect effect modification because it typically shows different effects in each stratum.
educationalObjective: Effect modification occurs when the magnitude or direction of the effect of the independent variable on the dependent variable (outcome) varies depending on the level of a third variable (effect modifier). Separate (stratified) analyses should be conducted for each level of the effect modifier.

explanations.A: Because the corresponding ORs are <1, alcohol and smoking are associated with a significant decrease in the odds of fecundability (whereas caffeine is not associated with fecundability because its CI included the null value).

• Alcohol (≥1 drinks/day vs <1 drink/day): OR = 0.20; 95% CI: 0.07 to 0.56
• Smoking (current smoker vs nonsmoker): OR = 0.34; 95% CI: 0.23 to 0.48
